title: Making Handoffs Easier to Receive
summary: What a handoff needs so the next person can start in minutes: status first, decisions with reasons, named risks, a clear next step, and a playback from the receiver.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The handoff message has three links and one line: "Everything should be in there." Technically, it is. The design file is there, the pull request is there, the ticket is there. The person picking it up still spends their first hour working out what changed, what's risky, what was already decided and which detail is still waiting on someone. Nobody did anything wrong. The sender just shipped the files and kept the map in their head.

Handoffs happen all the time in software: someone goes on leave, rotates off a project, finishes their shift on call, or passes a feature from design to dev to QA. Each one is a moment where context can leak. This post is about the receiving end: what a handoff needs so the next person can act in the first ten minutes instead of the first afternoon.

Hospitals have worked on this for years

Medicine has studied handoffs for years, because a shift change on a hospital ward is a handoff with real stakes. Two formats from that world are worth borrowing.

SBAR comes from Michael Leonard and colleagues at Kaiser Permanente of Colorado, and the Institute for Healthcare Improvement publishes it as a free tool. It has four parts: Situation (a short statement of the problem), Background (only the history that matters), Assessment (what you found and what you think) and Recommendation (what you want the other person to do).

I-PASS goes further. It stands for Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness and contingency planning, and Synthesis by receiver. In a 2014 study across nine hospitals with pediatric residency programs, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, rolling out I-PASS with training was followed by a 23% drop in medical errors (24.5 to 18.8 per 100 admissions) and a 30% drop in preventable adverse events. Oral handoffs didn't get longer, either (Boston Children's Hospital summary of the study).

Software isn't a hospital ward, and nobody's life depends on your migration ticket. The shape still carries over well: say where things stand, give only the background that changes decisions, name the risks, say what should happen next, and have the receiver play it back.

Five things a receivable handoff carries

Start with the current state in plain words: done, not done, blocked, risky, waiting on someone. Those few words orient the reader before the links start multiplying. Without them, every link is a room the receiver has to search alone.

Then the decisions that still shape the work, each with its reason. Nobody needs a transcript of every meeting. They need the history that changes what they'll do next:

  • "We went with the lighter migration because the full one needs product sign-off."
  • "We kept the old status field because the mobile app still reads it."
  • "The analytics event is on hold until naming is agreed with the data team."

Without the "because," the next person may undo a decision that took a week to reach.

Third, risks. It's tempting to send only the polished parts, as if doubt makes the work look weaker. In practice a named risk is a gift: the receiver can test it, watch it, escalate it or decide to accept it. An unnamed risk shows up later as a surprise, with less time to deal with it. If your handoff has a lot of open questions, the sibling post Making Handoffs Honest About What Is Unknown goes deeper on writing those down.

Fourth, the next action, stated plainly and near the top. "Review the fixture update." "Run the import scenario against staging." "Confirm the copy with legal." "Close the ticket once the live URL returns 200." If the receiver has to dig the next step out of ten paragraphs, the handoff is still doing too little.

Fifth, who to ask. A name for each open thread: the PM for scope, the backend owner for the API change, you for the next two days until you're properly off.

A handoff note that fits in one message

Status: import works on staging. Export not started. Blocked on the API rate limit answer.
Decided: kept the old status field (mobile still reads it). Lighter migration, full one needs PM sign-off.
Risks: big CSV files over 50 MB untested.
Next: run the import scenario on staging with the large fixture.
Ask: Lan for scope, Minh for the API, me until Friday.

Let the receiver say it back

The last letter of I-PASS is the one software teams skip: synthesis by receiver. The person taking over repeats the key points in their own words and asks questions while the sender is still around. In a team it can be a five-minute call or a reply in the thread: "So the next step is the large-file import on staging, and I shouldn't touch the status field. Right?" If the playback is off, you just found a gap in the note, and it cost one message instead of a broken deploy.

The tone matters too. A handoff isn't a report proving how much you did. It's there to make the next person's start easier, which usually means fewer impressive details and more pointers: where to start, what to trust, what to double-check, who to ask.

There's a little humility in all this. Your memory isn't part of the system. If the work can only continue when someone pings you to recover old context, the handoff isn't finished. The work should carry enough of its own story to survive a change of hands.

Before your next handoff

  • Put a one-line status before any link.
  • Write each open decision with its "because."
  • Name at least one risk, even if it feels small.
  • Ask the receiver to say the next step back to you before you sign off.

faqs.q: What should a good handoff include?
faqs.a: Five things: the current state in plain words (done, blocked, waiting), the decisions that still shape the work with the reason for each, the known risks, the next action stated near the top, and who to ask about each open thread. Links to the code, ticket and designs come after that orientation, not instead of it.

faqs.q: Are there proven handoff formats teams can borrow?
faqs.a: Yes, from medicine. SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) came out of Kaiser Permanente of Colorado and is published by the Institute for Healthcare Improvement. I-PASS adds an action list, contingency planning and a playback by the receiver; a 2014 NEJM study in nine hospitals found medical errors fell 23% and preventable adverse events 30% after it was introduced with training.

faqs.q: Why should the receiver repeat the handoff back?
faqs.a: Playback, which I-PASS calls synthesis by receiver, catches gaps while the sender is still available. If the receiver's summary of the next step or the key decisions is off, you fix the note with one message instead of discovering the gap after a broken deploy.

faqs.q: Doesn't writing down risks make the work look unfinished?
faqs.a: It makes the work easier to continue. A named risk lets the receiver test it, monitor it, escalate it or accept it on purpose. An unnamed risk tends to surface later as a surprise, when there is less time to handle it.
